opportunity: Target 18-24 instead of teens, add a freemium tier with 3 tasks and AI photo checks against cheating, plus friend streaks.

opportunity: Keep the simplicity, but add milestone badges, an urge log, shareable progress cards and optionally an accountability partner; widget as a free entry point, monetize the social layer and stats.

developer_type: solo: Roger You (individual), 5 apps; a review says the dev personally replies on Instagram

Borderline only because of the religious domain; the mechanic is fully transferable to secular habits.
monetization: Subscription (currently annual); some users accept paying and ask for a monthly plan, others refuse because the free tier is almost nothing.
opportunity: Same mechanic (pact + stake + photo proof) for secular Gen Z habits: gym, running, reading, studying; couples and friends as a distribution channel.

developer_type: small team (Quittr, LLC, 1 app)

developer_type: small team (Airix LLC, 3 apps, no tracking label; one review mentions lots of ads)

developer_type: small team (Crunchy Bagel Pty Ltd, 5 apps; estimate: small studio)
what_sets_it_apart: A classic habit tracker reduced to a streak of consecutive days, with strong Apple Watch and Health integration (automatic check-off) and a one-time price instead of a subscription.

developer_type: solo: the description says 'I'm a solo developer', Samtark Pty Ltd, 2 apps
what_sets_it_apart: A fasting timer that shows body phases live (ketosis, fat burning, autophagy) hour by hour, with a generous free tier without ads or an account. Borderline due to eating-disorder risk and weaker fit with the Gen Z narrative.
monetization: Freemium: basics free without ads; Pro subscription ~$9.99/mo or $49.99/yr (from a review); some users ask for a one-time purchase.

developer_type: small team (estimate): Nora Studios Inc, 2 apps
what_sets_it_apart: A gamified quit app (porn, sugar, social media) where the day streak grows as an interactive 3D orb, with hypnosis, an AI coach and a community. Borderline due to a hard paywall that users reject and clear signs of paid marketing.
